note: A general description of computing and software roles. It is not a job description or hiring requirement from any company and is not used for measurement or scoring.

ROLE_DEV_V1.summary: Taking requirements, setting module boundaries and interfaces, and writing code that works within that structure
ROLE_DEV_V1.practiceWhere: in a team project or your capstone build

TD01.why: Splitting requirements into modules and setting interface contracts is where design and development roles decide the structure.
TD01.ctx: in the design phase of a team project

TD03.why: Building server features that receive, process and respond to requests is where the structure you chose becomes real code.
TD03.ctx: when you build a web service assignment or your capstone server

out.J7: Record of narrowing down a cause

TD05.why: Implementing UI state and input handling is how you set the structure on the side users actually see.
TD05.ctx: in an assignment with a user interface or an app project

J1.task: At the start of a project, separate the features this system will handle from the ones you will not build this time, and write both at the top of the requirements list.
J1.check: Are the features you decided not to build listed with the reasons?

J2.task: Pick out the conditions you must meet, such as response time, concurrent users and supported devices, and rewrite them as statements you can verify.
J2.output: List of conditions and acceptance criteria
J2.check: Does every condition have a way to check it was met?

J3.task: Decide yourself where to split modules and which way dependencies point, and record why you chose one option and rejected the others in a decision record.
J3.check: Can you explain why you did not choose a different boundary?

J4.task: Try two libraries or frameworks that could do the same job on a small example, and decide which to use.
J4.check: Did you write the comparison criteria (learning cost, documentation, maintenance status and so on) before comparing?

J5.task: Write the interface contract down so teammates can integrate with your code without opening it.
J5.check: Are the request and response formats and every error case written down?

J6.task: Compare two implementations on the same input and the same criteria (code size, how much changes when you modify it, run time) and pick one.
J6.check: Were the two implementations compared under the same conditions?

J7.task: Find a case where changing one feature touched many files, redraw the boundaries, and check whether the change footprint shrank.
J7.output: Before and after record of the restructuring
J7.check: Did you count changed files before and after on the same basis?

J8.task: Record whether teammates started building from your contract or diagram, and what questions came up when they did.
J8.output: Record of contract use and questions
J8.check: Does it say who built which part from that contract?

responsibilities: Analysing requirements and setting feature scope
Designing module structure and interfaces
Implementing server and UI features and reviewing code
Fixing bugs and improving the structure of existing code

process.what: Product or the customer describes the features they want, in words or as screen sketches.
You separate the requirements you will take on from those you will not this time, and write down the conditions to meet.
You set module boundaries and interface contracts and keep a decision record.
You write the code, add tests and get it reviewed by colleagues.
You connect it with other modules and hand it to test and deployment.
You take bugs found in production and new requirements and adjust the structure.

tools: Git and the pull request and code review features of your code host
An IDE and debugger
Web frameworks and API description formats (OpenAPI and similar)
Diagram notations such as UML
experiences: Owning one module in a team project from start to finish
Reading and modifying code someone else wrote
Giving and receiving code reviews and fixing what was pointed out
entry: Take on the design document in a software engineering or web programming team assignment
In your capstone, define the interface of one server or front-end module yourself
Pick a small issue in an open-source repository, fix it and go through the review process

learnOrder.step: Finishing a small program in one language
learnOrder.why: Before you can think about structure, you need one language you are comfortable in.
In professional development you spend more time merging with other people's code than writing alone.
Even a new hire's first tasks are judged on whether you can explain the boundaries of the module you own.
The habit of not breaking other things when you change code is the basis of maintenance.

firstProject.title: Build a small web service as three modules
firstProject.goal: Split a small service such as a to-do manager into UI, server and storage modules that can be connected using only their contracts
steps: Write the features you will and will not build on a one-page requirements list
Write a contract for the boundaries of the three modules and the request and response formats they exchange
Implement each module and confirm with tests that it behaves according to the contract
Add one feature, count how many modules changed, and review the structure
firstProject.output: Requirements list, module diagram and interface contracts, and a repository with tests
firstProject.check: When you added a feature, did only one module change, and if several did, can you explain why?

portfolio: A module diagram with the reasons for drawing the boundaries that way
An interface contract someone else built against
One page on the requirements you chose not to take on and why

interview.q: When you split modules, what criteria did you use to set the boundaries?
interview.why: The basis for your structure shows your design habits.

interview.q: What did you leave behind so others could use your code?
interview.why: Development does not end with you and carries on to the next person through contracts and documents.

interview.q: If a change ever broke something else, how did you find it and prevent it?
interview.why: Narrowing down the impact of a change is a habit you use every day at work.

postingCheck: Whether the role is backend, frontend or mobile
Whether the posting names the languages and frameworks
Whether the focus is building new things or maintaining existing systems
ROLE_DEV_V1.watch: Development postings are split by title, such as Backend Engineer, Frontend Engineer or Mobile Developer. Rather than listing languages, show that you set the boundaries of a module you owned and handed it over in a form others could use. That works for any of these postings.

ROLE_PERF_V1.summary: Measuring and predicting processing time and resource needs before building or changing something, and providing the evidence for where to make changes
ROLE_PERF_V1.practiceWhere: in algorithms or database assignments or performance checks on your capstone

TD02.why: Working out the complexity of data representations and algorithms and comparing it with measurements is the core of an analysis and estimation role.
TD02.ctx: in algorithms course assignments or coding labs

TD04.why: Narrowing down why a query is slow through execution plans and indexes, a place where service performance often wobbles.
TD04.ctx: in database course assignments or the storage layer of a project

out.J6: Query time before and after indexing

TD07.why: Measuring latency and throughput between machines is how you set the capacity needed as users grow.
TD07.ctx: in networking labs or server load tests

J1.task: When someone says it is slow, first pin down and write which feature and which input size is slow.
J1.check: Does it also say which features and input ranges you will not measure this time?

J2.task: Rewrite a requirement such as it must be fast as numeric conditions such as response time, throughput and a memory ceiling.
J2.check: Does every condition have a measurement method and a target value?

J3.task: Look at the measurements, pick one bottleneck, and write down the evidence for that call.
J3.check: Did you write why you did not treat the other candidates as the bottleneck?

J4.task: Look at the same problem two ways, by calculating theoretical complexity and by measuring real time, and decide which to use as evidence.
J4.check: Did you record the measurement setup (input size, number of runs, machine)?

J5.task: Write up your measurements and predictions as a report someone else could read and use to change the design.
J5.check: Can a reader tell what to change and how much difference it will make?

J6.task: Compare the value you predicted before a change with the value you measured after it, under the same conditions.
J6.check: Did you measure with the same input and the same environment?

J7.task: Pick one prediction that missed, narrow down which assumption was wrong, and fix your prediction method.
J7.output: Note on why the prediction missed
J7.check: Do you have evidence that narrows it to one wrong assumption?

J8.task: Record how your analysis fed into team decisions such as a structural change or the number of servers.
J8.check: Does it say which measurement was used for which decision?

responsibilities: Measuring response time and resource use of services and programs
Analysing bottlenecks and proposing improvements
Capacity planning for user growth
Reviewing database queries and indexes

process.what: Development or operations raises problems such as it has got slower, or users will grow next month.
You decide what to measure, with which inputs and how many times, and set up a consistent environment.
You measure time and resources with profilers and load tests and narrow down bottleneck candidates.
You calculate how much a fix will help and what will run out first as users grow.
You hand improvements and capacity criteria to development and operations, with the evidence.
After the fix you measure again, check whether the prediction held, and adjust your prediction method.

knowledge: Computer architecture and operating systems (caches, memory, threads)
Basic statistics for reading measurements (mean, variance, percentiles)
tools: Profilers (language-specific profilers, Linux perf and similar)
Load testing tools (JMeter, k6 and similar)
Database execution plans (EXPLAIN)
Spreadsheets or Python plotting for charting measurements
experiences: Measuring the run time of assignment code by input size and plotting it
Finding and fixing a slow part and comparing before and after
Fixing your assumptions after a prediction missed
entry: In an algorithms assignment, measure and compare the run time of two solutions by input size
In a database assignment, measure query times before and after adding an index
Run a load test on your capstone server and find where response time starts to climb

learnOrder.why: Calculation is the first basis for a prediction, and only measurement tells you whether it is right.
If you compare two measurements taken under different conditions, no conclusion can be trusted.
The bottleneck is more often where the tool points than where you guessed.
For an analysis to inform a decision, it has to become a document others can read.

firstProject.title: Write a performance analysis report for one project server
firstProject.goal: Measure the response time of a service you built, find one bottleneck, and compare your prediction with the measurement after the fix
steps: Pick two or three key requests and set numeric response time targets
Run a load test, increasing concurrent requests, and measure response time and resource use
Pick one bottleneck and write down beforehand how much you expect fixing it to help
After the fix, measure again under the same conditions and put prediction and measurement in one table
firstProject.output: A report containing the performance targets, measurement records and a predicted versus measured table
firstProject.check: Can you explain with measurements why the prediction held or missed?

portfolio: A performance analysis report
A predicted versus measured comparison table
One page on the evidence that identified the bottleneck

interview.q: How did you find the slow part? Was it a guess or a measurement?
interview.why: The habit of narrowing down by measurement is where this role starts.

interview.q: If you predicted the speed-up before making a change, how close was the real result?
interview.why: Having compared prediction with measurement is the evidence behind an analysis role.

interview.q: Whose decision did your analysis feed into, and which one?
interview.why: An analysis counts as an achievement when it was used for someone's decision.

postingCheck: Whether performance here means servers and databases or devices and embedded systems
Whether capacity planning or load testing are listed as duties
Whether it hires graduates or experienced developers
ROLE_PERF_V1.watch: Graduate roles that do only performance analysis are rare. People more often join as backend, systems or database developers and take on performance work, so it is realistic to look for duties such as performance improvement or load testing in development postings. Titles you may see include Performance Engineer and Capacity Planning Engineer.

ROLE_QA_V1.summary: Deciding what to test and where the pass line sits, and judging whether the release about to go out clears it
ROLE_QA_V1.practiceWhere: in the test phase of a team project or a software engineering assignment

TD10.why: Setting test items and pass criteria and running automated tests is where test and verification roles make their call.
TD10.ctx: in the test phase of a team project

TD05.why: Handling UI input and edge cases produces many test items, because the interface is where users meet defects first.
TD05.ctx: in an assignment with a user interface or an app project

TD03.why: Checking that requests and responses follow the contract is how you build a server-side test suite.
TD03.ctx: in the server part of a web service assignment

J1.task: Before testing starts, separate the features you will test in this release from those you will not, and write both down.
J1.check: Are the untested areas listed with the reasons?

J2.task: Turn a requirement such as it should work properly into test items with inputs and expected results.
J2.check: Does every item have a single expected result?

J3.task: Decide yourself which boundary inputs to test (empty values, the longest value, malformed input) and set the pass criteria.
J3.check: Can you explain why you drew the line where you did?

J4.task: Test the same feature two ways, by hand and with automated tests, and decide how much to automate.
J4.check: Does it give the reason for each item you chose not to automate?

J5.task: Leave a test suite and defect reports that a teammate could download and run as they are.
J5.check: Could someone reproduce the defect from your report alone?

J6.task: Check the test results against the pass criteria table and judge this release as pass or hold.
J6.check: For every held item, does it say which criterion it failed?

J7.task: Pick a defect that slipped through testing, narrow down why it was not caught, and add a test that catches that case.
J7.output: Record of the gap and the added test
J7.check: Did you confirm the new test actually catches that defect?

J8.task: Record how your verdict was used in the team's decision to present or release.
J8.check: Does it say who used the verdict for which decision?

responsibilities: Writing test plans and test items from the requirements
Running functional and regression tests and reporting defects
Writing and maintaining automated tests
Making the pre-release call and reporting on quality status

process.what: From the requirements documents and schedule, you set the test scope and criteria for this release.
For each feature you write test items split into normal, boundary and error cases.
You run manual and automated tests and record the results.
You file defects with reproduction steps and agree the fix order with development.
You test the fixed build again and run regression tests to check nothing else broke.
You check against the pass criteria and report whether it can be released.

knowledge: Software engineering (requirements analysis and test phases)
Test design techniques (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis)
How web and mobile apps work (requests and responses, UI state)
tools: Unit test frameworks (JUnit, pytest and similar)
UI automation tools (Selenium, Playwright and similar)
API testing tools (Postman and similar)
Defect management tools and issue trackers
experiences: Writing and running test items yourself on a team project
Reporting a defect so someone else could reproduce it
Adding an escaped defect to the tests so it would not come back
entry: Take on the test plan and test items in a software engineering course assignment
Add automated tests to your capstone and run them every time the code changes
Learn test terminology and design techniques from the ISTQB Foundation Level (CTFL) syllabus

learnOrder.why: Testing starts with writing down what you expect.

learnOrder.step: Boundary value analysis and equivalence partitioning
learnOrder.why: You cannot test every input, so you need criteria for choosing.
A defect nobody can reproduce is one development cannot fix.
If you run the same tests by hand every time, something gets missed with each new build.

firstProject.title: Own the test plan and verdict for one feature of a team project
firstProject.goal: Pick one feature, set its test items and pass criteria, and judge pass or hold from the test results
steps: Read the requirements for one feature and write the scope you will and will not test
Write test items and expected results split into normal, boundary and error cases
Run the tests and report the defects you find with reproduction steps
Check against the pass criteria table, make the call, and add any missed cases to the next round
firstProject.output: Test scope note, test items and pass criteria table, defect reports and verdict record
firstProject.check: If you judged hold, can you point to the item and the criterion it failed?

portfolio: A set of test items and a pass criteria table
A defect report someone else reproduced
One page on the scope you did not cover

interview.q: Since you cannot test every input, what did you choose to test?
interview.why: Your criteria for choosing test scope show your judgement.

interview.q: When you separated pass from hold, what did you base the call on?
interview.why: Having made verdicts is the evidence behind a test role.

interview.q: If something passed testing and a defect appeared later, what did you change?
interview.why: This looks at whether you habitually feed escaped cases back into the tests.

postingCheck: Whether the role is mainly manual testing or includes writing automated test code
Whether you would test web, mobile or devices
Whether experience with a programming language is required
ROLE_QA_V1.watch: What test roles cover varies a lot between companies. Some, often titled QA Tester or QA Analyst, are mainly manual testing, while others, such as QA Engineer, SDET or Test Automation Engineer, are close to development roles that write test code. Use the duties in the posting to work out which kind it is first.

ROLE_DEPLOY_V1.summary: Setting procedures and environments so the same code produces the same artefact whenever and wherever it is built, and creating a deployment path that can be rolled back when something goes wrong
ROLE_DEPLOY_V1.practiceWhere: while managing a team project repository or deploying your capstone server

TD10.why: Automating build, test and deploy steps and setting rollback paths is what build and deployment automation roles work on every day.

TD06.why: Working with the operating system, processes and resource settings is the foundation for writing environment configuration as code.
TD06.ctx: in Linux or operating systems labs

TD07.why: Rolling out across several servers and changing a service without stopping it is what you use when splitting a deployment into stages.
TD07.ctx: when you roll a service out across several servers

J1.task: Before starting deployment work, separate the steps you will automate this time from those you will leave manual, and write both down.
J1.check: Are the manual steps listed with the reasons?

J2.task: Rewrite a requirement such as deployment must be safe as conditions such as tests passing, build time and time to roll back.
J2.check: Does every condition have a way to check it?

J3.task: Decide yourself how many stages the deployment has and where it should stop, and record why.
J3.output: Deployment stages and stop conditions table
J3.check: Are the stop conditions written as criteria you can check?

J4.task: Run the same build two ways (a shell script and a container, or two CI tools) and decide which to use.
J4.check: Did you write the comparison criteria before comparing?

J5.task: Leave the procedure and configuration files so a new teammate could build and deploy from a single page of documentation.
J5.output: Deployment procedure document and configuration files
J5.check: Did another teammate follow it and succeed?

J6.task: Build the same commit twice and on another machine, and compare whether the artefacts match.
J6.check: Where differences appeared, did you write why?

J7.task: Deliberately create a post-deployment failure, roll back to the previous version, and fix any step that got stuck.
J7.check: After rolling back, did you confirm the service runs as it did before?

J8.task: Record whether the deployment procedure you built became the team's standard way of working, and who uses it.
J8.check: Does it say who deploys with that procedure and since when?

responsibilities: Building and maintaining build, test and deployment automation (CI/CD)
Setting up and managing development, test and production environments
Designing deployment stages and providing rollback paths
Helping developers with build and deployment problems

process.what: Development asks how a new service or a changed architecture should be rolled out.
You set the operating system, runtime and configuration needed and write them as code.
You chain the build, test and deploy stages in a CI tool.
You deploy to a test environment first and check that the stop condition at each stage works.
You roll out to some servers or some users first and widen it while watching the metrics.
You practise the rollback path for when something goes wrong and fix the procedure.

knowledge: Operating systems and Linux basics (processes, permissions, file systems)
Shell scripting and one programming language
tools: Git and CI tools (GitHub Actions, Jenkins and similar)
Containers (Docker) and container orchestration basics (Kubernetes and similar)
Basics of infrastructure-as-code tools
The Linux command line
experiences: Adding automated builds and tests to a team repository
Bringing up a project server yourself and writing a procedure anyone could use to bring it up again
Rolling back to a previous version after a problem appeared post-deployment
entry: Add an automated pipeline to your team project repository that runs the tests on every commit
Package your capstone server in a container so it runs the same on anyone's machine
Build command-line and system administration basics by preparing for an entry-level Linux certification

learnOrder.step: The Linux command line and shell scripting
learnOrder.why: Most deployment work happens on a server's command line.
What goes out and when is decided by the flow of the repository.
Writing the environment as code is what lets you produce the same result again and again.
When a real incident happens, you use the way back before the way forward.

firstProject.title: Build a one-step deploy and rollback path for your capstone service
firstProject.goal: Make commits trigger test, build and deploy in sequence, with a way to roll back to the previous version when something goes wrong
steps: Write the environment the service needs as configuration files and package it in a container
Add an automated pipeline to the repository that runs tests and builds on every commit
Separate test and production deployments and set a stop condition for each stage
Deploy a deliberately broken version, roll it back and record any step that got stuck
firstProject.output: Environment configuration files, pipeline configuration, a deployment stages table and a rollback drill record
firstProject.check: Could another teammate produce the same artefact and roll it back from the documentation alone?

portfolio: A deployment procedure with the reason for each stage's stop condition
Environment configuration code
One page on the rollback path and your drill record

interview.q: If you split deployment into stages, where did you make it stop, and why there?
interview.why: Where you put stop conditions shows how you see risk.

interview.q: Has the same code ever behaved differently on another machine? How did you make them match?
interview.why: A build that gives the same result every time is where this role starts.

interview.q: When a problem appeared after deployment, how did you roll back?
interview.why: Rollback experience is one of the first things checked in practice.

postingCheck: Whether the posting is titled DevOps, Platform or Infrastructure, and what the actual duties say
Whether it names the cloud and container tools used
Whether development experience is required first
ROLE_DEPLOY_V1.watch: Build and deployment automation is advertised under titles such as DevOps Engineer, Platform Engineer and Infrastructure Engineer. Graduate openings are often bundled with development or operations, so keep evidence in your repository history that you did this work on a team project.

ROLE_SRE_V1.summary: Setting metrics and alert thresholds so a released service does not stop, and when an incident happens, narrowing down the cause, restoring service and preventing recurrence
ROLE_SRE_V1.practiceWhere: while running your capstone server or looking after a club or society's service

TD07.why: Measuring latency and dropouts across machines and network segments and narrowing down the cause is what service operations looks at first in an incident.
TD07.ctx: in networking labs or a project that runs across several servers

TD10.why: Monitoring metrics, alert thresholds and incident records are the tools and documents operations uses every day.
TD10.ctx: after your capstone service has been released

out.J2: Uptime targets and alert thresholds table
out.J7: Incident record and recurrence prevention note

TD03.why: Reading the request handling flow and error logs is how you narrow down where inside the server an incident happened.
TD03.ctx: using server logs and error responses as evidence

J1.task: When you take on operations, set and write down the service scope you will protect (which features, which hours) and what you will not cover this time.
J1.check: Is the scope you will not cover listed with the reasons?

J2.task: Rewrite a requirement such as it must not go down as targets such as uptime percentage, response time and allowable downtime.
J2.check: Does every target have the metric and the period it is measured over?

J3.task: Decide yourself which metric crossing which value should fire an alert, and who responds first.
J3.check: Did you consider alerts that fire too often or fail to fire when they should?

J4.task: Look at the same incident two ways, through logs and through metric graphs, and decide which to use first to narrow down the cause.
J4.check: Did you write the limit of the method you chose in one line?

J5.task: Write an incident response procedure that someone seeing it for the first time could follow.
J5.check: Are where to look, who to contact and how to roll back written in order?

J6.task: Compare a month of uptime records with the targets you set at the start, on the same basis.
J6.check: Are the targets and records on the same metric and the same period?

J7.task: Pick one incident, narrow down the cause segment by segment, and write what you will change so it does not happen again.
J7.output: Incident record and recurrence prevention note
J7.check: Does the record contain the evidence that narrowed it to one cause?

J8.task: Record how your operations records fed into team decisions such as adding servers or changing the architecture.
J8.check: Does it say which record was used for which decision?

responsibilities: Setting service monitoring metrics and alerts
Incident response, root cause analysis and recurrence prevention
Capacity reviews and deciding when to scale
Automating operational tasks and documenting response procedures

process.what: For each service you set the uptime level and response time to maintain.
You collect metrics and logs and set alert thresholds.
When an alert fires, you check the scope of impact first and restore the service by rolling back or routing around the problem.
You narrow down the cause segment by segment and write the incident record.
You change configuration, procedures or architecture so the same thing does not happen again.
You look at the accumulated records and decide when to scale and what it will cost.

knowledge: Operating systems and Linux (processes, memory, disk)
Basic statistics for measuring uptime targets (means, percentiles)
tools: The Linux command line and system monitoring tools
Monitoring and visualisation tools (Prometheus, Grafana and similar)
Log collection and search tools
Shell scripts or Python to automate operational tasks
experiences: Running a server you set up yourself for a period and watching its metrics
Finding the cause and restoring service when it went down
Writing an incident record and applying a recurrence fix
entry: Run your capstone service until the end of the semester with monitoring graphs and alerts attached
In a networking lab, use a packet analyser to find the segment where latency and dropouts occur
Build systems and networking basics by preparing for an entry-level Linux or networking certification

learnOrder.why: The cause of an incident usually shows up somewhere in these two layers.
You can only spot an anomaly if you know what normal looks like.

learnOrder.step: Writing alert thresholds and response procedures
learnOrder.why: Even an alert at 3 a.m. should be something you can handle by following the document.
Making sure you never go through the same incident twice is a large part of operations.

firstProject.title: Keep a semester-long operations log for your capstone service
firstProject.goal: Attach targets and alerts to a released service, and record the problems that occur as incident records with recurrence fixes
steps: Set uptime and response time targets and write how you will measure them
Attach monitoring graphs and alerts and write down the alert thresholds
Every time a problem occurs, record the scope of impact, the cause and the recovery
At the end of the semester, compare the records with the targets and write up what to change
firstProject.output: Uptime targets table, alert thresholds and response procedure, a set of incident records and a semester operations comparison
firstProject.check: For each incident, can you trace from the records how you narrowed the cause and what you changed?

portfolio: A set of operational metrics and alert thresholds
Incident records and recurrence fixes
One page setting out the escalation steps

interview.q: When the service went down, what did you check first?
interview.why: This looks at whether you check the scope of impact first and then narrow down segment by segment.

interview.q: If you have set alert thresholds yourself, what did you base the values on?
interview.why: Alert thresholds show the basis for your operational judgement.

interview.q: If you had to put a reliable service into numbers, what would you measure?
interview.why: This looks at your instinct for making operational targets measurable.

postingCheck: Whether the posting is titled Site Reliability Engineer, Systems Operations or Infrastructure Operations
Whether night or on-call shifts are part of the job
Whether writing automation code for operations is required
ROLE_SRE_V1.watch: Depending on company size, service operations is either combined with development or kept separate. Graduates often start in operations support or infrastructure operations, so prepare using records from a service you have actually run.

ROLE_PM_V1.summary: Gathering requirements from many people, deciding what to build first and what not to take on, and matching schedule and staffing to carry development through to the end
ROLE_PM_V1.practiceWhere: as team lead or scheduler on a team project or capstone

TD01.why: Gathering requirements, drawing the scope and deciding what not to take on is the first thing integration and coordination roles handle.
TD01.ctx: in the planning phase of a team project

TD04.why: Organising requirements such as what data to hold, how it will be searched and how long it is kept is how a coordination role checks requirements down to the data fields.
TD04.ctx: when you turn the requirements list into data fields

TD10.why: Deciding whether to ship by looking at release criteria and test results is where you compare the promised scope with what was delivered.
TD10.ctx: ahead of a team project presentation or release

J1.task: At the start of a project, agree with your team what you will and will not build this semester, and write it down.
J1.check: Are the things you decided not to build listed with the reasons?

J2.task: Gather requirements from your supervisor, teammates and expected users, and turn them into a list with priorities and done criteria.
J2.check: Does every requirement have a criterion for when it counts as done?

J3.task: Decide yourself the build order and who owns what, and write one line on why each deferred requirement was deferred.
J3.output: Schedule and roles table with a rationale note
J3.check: Can you explain why you deferred each deferred requirement?

J4.task: Try two ways of tracking requirements and tasks (an issue tracker, a kanban board, a spreadsheet) and decide which the team will use.
J4.check: Did you write the drawback of the method you chose in one line?

J5.task: Record decisions from meetings and changed requirements in a change log every teammate can see.
J5.check: For every changed requirement, does it say who changed it, when and why?

J6.task: At mid-semester and at the end, put the scope you originally promised and what you actually built on the same list and compare.
J6.check: Does every missing feature have a reason?

J7.task: Pick a moment when the schedule slipped, redraw the scope, and write what you will change in the next plan.
J7.check: Is there a basis for what you cut and what you kept?

J8.task: Record how you reached agreement between teammates or users who disagreed, and what that agreement decided.
J8.check: Does it say who agreed to what and which decision the agreement fed into?

responsibilities: Gathering requirements from customers, users and internal teams and setting priorities
Planning development schedule and staffing and tracking progress
Handling requirement changes and coordinating stakeholders
Finalising release scope and reviewing results

process.what: The features customers, product and operations want arrive through documents or meetings.
You separate the requirements you will take on from those you will not and set priorities.
You set the build order, schedule and owners and align them with the team.
Each week you review progress and clear blockers or adjust the scope.
You weigh the impact and cost of requirements that arrive midway and accept or defer them.
You compare the promised scope with the results and feed that into the plan for the next release.

knowledge: Ways of running development such as Agile and Scrum
Basics of databases and system architecture
Basics of schedule and risk management
tools: Issue trackers and kanban boards (Jira and similar)
Shared document tools and meeting note templates
UI design tools (Figma and similar) to agree requirements visually
Spreadsheets for managing schedule and scope
experiences: Acting as team lead or scheduler on a team project
Setting priorities and reaching agreement when requirements conflicted
Cutting scope because the schedule slipped
entry: Take charge of the requirements list and change log in your capstone
Write the requirements analysis and schedule yourself in a software engineering course
Gather user requirements for a campus service or a club app and try setting priorities

learnOrder.step: Writing requirements as a list with done criteria
learnOrder.why: Every coordination decision starts from what you agreed to build.
You need to speak developers' language to set a realistic schedule and scope.
The call coordination roles make most often is what to cut.
If the reasons for changes are recorded, you can trace afterwards where things went off course.

firstProject.title: Manage the requirements list and change log for a semester of your capstone
firstProject.goal: Turn your team's requirements into a prioritised list, record requirement changes, and compare promises with results at the end of the semester
steps: Gather requirements from the team, your supervisor and expected users into one list
Add a priority and done criterion to each requirement and decide which you will not take on this time
Record requirements that change during the semester in the change log, with who changed them and why
At the end of the semester, compare the promised scope with what was built and write up why items are missing
firstProject.output: Prioritised requirements list, change log and promised scope versus results table
firstProject.check: For every requirement you declined or deferred, can you show from the records why you decided that?

portfolio: A requirements list with the criteria you used to set priorities
A change log
One page on the requirements you chose not to take on and why

interview.q: When requirements conflicted, what did you decide to do first? What were your criteria?
interview.why: Your criteria for priorities show your coordination judgement.

interview.q: When the schedule slipped, what did you cut and what did you keep?
interview.why: Redrawing the scope is the experience used most often in practice.

interview.q: Have you reached agreement between people who disagreed?
interview.why: Coordination is less about deciding alone and more about getting others to follow.

postingCheck: Whether PM here means product management or development scheduling and project management
Whether development experience or technical understanding is required
Whether working with client companies (contract development) is part of the job
ROLE_PM_V1.watch: Integration and coordination roles go by a mix of titles, such as Product Manager, Technical Project Manager and Project Coordinator, and graduate openings are relatively few. People often join through development or testing and widen into coordination work, so keep records of owning requirements and schedules on team projects. They will be useful whichever route you take.

ROLE_RESEARCH_V1.summary: Narrowing down a question that has no answer yet, and comparing a new method with a baseline under the same conditions to establish whether it works and how far
ROLE_RESEARCH_V1.practiceWhere: in a final-year thesis, as an undergraduate research assistant or in a machine learning project

TD09.why: Splitting data, training models and comparing them with a baseline is the core of an exploration and research role.
TD09.ctx: in machine learning coursework or a data analysis project

TD02.why: Weighing the computational cost and accuracy of a method is how you decide whether a new method is practical.
TD02.ctx: in algorithms assignments or lab experiments

out.J3: Note on why you chose the method

TD11.why: In fields such as graphics and image processing, results are judged by eye and by time together, which is where you check whether a researched method holds up under real-time constraints.
TD11.ctx: in graphics or image processing assignments

J1.task: Pick a question left open in a paper or assignment you read, and narrow the scope you will answer this time to one sentence.
J1.check: Is the scope you will not answer written down too?

J2.task: Before anything else, decide and write down how you will measure better: the evaluation metrics and the evaluation data.
J2.check: Are the reason for the metrics and how you split the evaluation data written down?

J3.task: When several methods are possible, pick one with a small experiment and record why you rejected the others.
J3.output: Note on why you chose the method
J3.check: Did you run the rejected methods under the same conditions too?

J4.task: Set and record the experimental conditions (data split, random seed, hyperparameters) and repeat runs under the same conditions.
J4.check: Could someone rerun the same experiment from your log alone?

J5.task: Package the experiment code, configuration and results in a repository and a short report others can rerun.
J5.check: Can someone follow it from installation through to the results table?

J6.task: Compare your method with the simplest baseline on the same data and the same metrics.
J6.check: Are the comparison conditions written in the table?

J7.task: Collect the cases where your method is wrong or does not work, find what they have in common, and rewrite the range where it works.
J7.output: Error case list and limitations note
J7.check: Can you show with examples where it does not work?

J8.task: Record how your results were used in other people's experiments in the lab or in team product decisions.
J8.check: Does it say who used them for which experiment or decision?

responsibilities: Framing research questions and surveying related papers
Designing experiments and implementing models and algorithms
Running comparison experiments against baselines and analysing results
Writing papers and technical reports and assessing product use

process.what: A problem to solve arrives as a product need or a research topic.
You read related papers and public implementations and separate what is solved from what remains.
You set the evaluation data, metrics and the baseline to compare against.
You implement the method, run it repeatedly under the same conditions and log the runs.
You compare with the baseline and collect failure cases to find the limits.
You write a report or paper, and if the method is worth using, hand it to development.

knowledge: Basics of machine learning and deep learning
tools: Python with numerical and data tools (NumPy, pandas)
Model libraries (PyTorch, scikit-learn and similar)
Experiment tracking and notebook environments (Jupyter and similar)
Paper writing tools (LaTeX)
experiences: Rerunning the results of a paper yourself
Comparing a baseline and your own method under the same conditions
Finding why an experiment failed and revising the question
entry: Join a lab as an undergraduate research assistant and take on reproducing one of its experiments
In a machine learning assignment, compare a baseline with your own method on public data
Pick a paper in your area, run its published code and rebuild its results table

learnOrder.why: They are the basis for understanding a paper's method and judging whether a difference in results can be trusted.
Getting someone else's result again builds the habit of writing down experimental conditions.
If the conditions are not the same, you cannot say it improved.
Knowing where a method does not work is part of the research result too.

firstProject.title: Reproduce a paper and change one thing
firstProject.goal: Rerun the experiments of a published paper to confirm the results, then change one condition and see how the results change
steps: Pick a paper in your area with public code and data, and write its research question in one sentence
Run it under the same conditions as the paper and compare how closely your results table matches
Change one of the data, metrics or settings and run it again alongside the baseline
Write up the changed results and the cases where it did not work in a short report
firstProject.output: Experiment log, reproduction results compared with the original paper, a condition change comparison table and a short report
firstProject.check: Could someone rebuild the same tables from your repository alone?

portfolio: A set of experimental conditions and results
A comparison table against the baseline
One page on where the method does not work

interview.q: How did you narrow down that research question? How does it differ from your first question?
interview.why: The process of narrowing the question shows your research judgement.

interview.q: How did you confirm it was better than the baseline?
interview.why: A fair comparison is what makes research results believable.

interview.q: When an experiment did not go as expected, what did you change?
interview.why: This looks at how you turn a failure into the next experiment.

postingCheck: Whether a master's degree or higher is required, or bachelor's graduates are accepted
Whether the focus is publishing papers or applying results to products
Which field it covers (vision, language, recommendation, graphics and so on)
ROLE_RESEARCH_V1.watch: Many research postings, such as Research Scientist or Research Engineer, ask for a graduate degree. As an undergraduate, build reproduction experience as a research assistant or lab intern, and it is realistic to also look at roles closer to product work, such as Machine Learning Engineer.

ROLE_QUALITY_V1.summary: Turning external quality and security standards into check items, judging with evidence whether a service keeps meeting them throughout operation, and making sure the same defect does not come back
ROLE_QUALITY_V1.practiceWhere: in security lab assignments or the review phase of a team project

TD08.why: Setting the assets to protect and the acceptable limits, and checking against the standard, is the basis on which quality and reliability roles make their calls.
TD08.ctx: in information security coursework or security labs

TD10.why: Collecting test results and incident records to see whether the same defect comes back is how you decide corrective action.
TD10.ctx: using your team project's defect records as evidence

TD06.why: Finding defects in memory handling and concurrent execution is how you narrow down the cause of defects that are rare but spread widely once they occur.

J1.task: At the start of a review, set and write down which parts of the system you will check this time and which you will not.
J1.check: Are the parts you did not check listed with the reasons?

J2.task: Turn a public security checklist (such as the OWASP Top 10) or a quality standard into check items you can verify on your system.
J2.check: Does every item say what you need to see for it to pass?

J3.task: From the issues the review found, decide yourself which to fix now and which risks to accept, and record why.
J3.check: Does every accepted risk have a reason and a date to revisit it?

J4.task: Choose the review methods (tool-based and manual) and the review interval, and run it once.
J4.check: Did you write how you covered the items the tools cannot catch?

J5.task: Record every verdict with its evidence so you can trace later what it was based on.
J5.check: Could someone reach the same verdict from the evidence alone?

J6.task: Check the review results against the standard item by item and judge each as compliant or non-compliant.
J6.check: For every non-compliant item, does it say which part of the standard it breaches?

J7.task: Pick a defect that kept recurring, narrow down the cause, change the procedure or configuration so it does not come back, and review again.
J7.check: Did you confirm the same defect does not come back after the change?

J8.task: Record how your verdict was used in the team's decision to hold or allow a release.
J8.output: Record of how verdicts were used
J8.check: Are the hold or allow decision and the evidence used at the time written down together?

responsibilities: Organising quality and security standards and maintaining check items
Regular reviews, vulnerability assessments and compliance verdicts
Analysing the causes of defects and incidents and managing corrective action
Preparing evidence for certification audits and other audits

process.what: Conditions to meet, such as laws, customer requirements and internal standards, arrive from outside.
You turn the standards into check items you can verify on your system.
You check with tools and by hand and record the results with evidence.
You mark each item compliant or non-compliant and decide which risks to accept.
You narrow down the cause of non-compliant items, fix them and review again.
You set a review interval and keep checking that the standards are met throughout operation.

knowledge: Information security basics (authentication, authorisation, cryptography, web vulnerabilities)
Basic concepts of relevant laws such as data protection laws (the GDPR, for example)
tools: Web vulnerability scanners (OWASP ZAP and similar) and static analysis tools
Memory checkers (Valgrind and similar) and race condition detectors
Tools for tracking defect and review history
Templates for check item tables and verdict records
experiences: Looking for vulnerabilities in a project service against a checklist
Narrowing down the cause of a recurring defect and preventing it
Comparing your system's state with a standard and writing a report
entry: In an information security course, review your team project service against a web vulnerability list
Collect your team project's defect records and track the cases where the same defect came back
Learn quality and security terms and standards by preparing for an entry-level security certification

learnOrder.step: Core concepts of security and quality
learnOrder.why: You can only build check items once you know what needs protecting.
Standards from outside are often written in sentences you cannot check as they are.
You need to know how to split what the tools catch from what a person has to look at.
A verdict can only be reused in audits and re-reviews if its evidence is kept.

firstProject.title: Write a quality and security review report for one team project service
firstProject.goal: Turn a public web vulnerability list into check items, review your service, then fix one non-compliant item and review again
steps: Set the review scope and turn the standard list into check items for your service
Check each item with tools and by hand and write down the result and evidence
Split the non-compliant items into those to fix now and risks to accept, and write down why
Fix one, review again and record whether the verdict changed
firstProject.output: Check items table, a review report with evidence, an accepted risk note and a corrective action and re-review record
firstProject.check: Can you show the evidence for every verdict, and point to whether the fixed item passed the re-review?

portfolio: A set of quality criteria and review results
A corrective action record
One page on the risks you accepted and why

interview.q: If you have judged compliance with a standard, what did you use as evidence?
interview.why: The habit of keeping the evidence for a verdict is the basis of this role.

interview.q: When you could not fix every issue straight away, what did you fix first?
interview.why: This looks at your judgement in choosing which risks to accept.

interview.q: If the same defect has come back, what did you change to stop it?
interview.why: Preventing recurrence is what separates Quality and Reliability from Test and Verification.

postingCheck: Whether quality assurance, security review or certification work carries the most weight
Whether compliance certifications such as ISO/IEC 27001 or SOC 2, or audit work, are listed
Whether security certifications are listed as a plus
ROLE_QUALITY_V1.watch: Quality and reliability work is split under different names at each company, such as Quality Assurance Engineer, Security Analyst and Compliance Engineer. Industries where outside bodies set the standards, such as finance and the public sector, take this work seriously, so it helps to decide on a target industry and search postings with it in mind.
